title_original: Vishwendra Singh Talks “Khoriya”, Nepali Migrants, Documentary Realism and Life on the Margins of Delhi

blocks.text: Vishwendra Singh Talks “Khoriya”, Nepali Migrants, Documentary Realism and Life on the Margins of Delhi
Vishwendra Singh discusses “Khoriya”, Nepali migrants, documentary realism and finding authenticity through actors and real locations.

Vishwendra Singh’s “ Khoriya ” emerged from an attempt to document a community that, despite being highly visible within Indian cities, remains largely absent from mainstream representation. Centered on Nepali migrants living and working in Delhi, the film combines fiction with an intensely observational approach, following characters whose financial insecurity, precarious employment and outsider status leave them almost permanently in motion. Speaking with Asian Movie Pulse, Singh discussed the documentary origins of the project, the connection between the film’s bird-flu outbreak and COVID, its relentless tension, working with Nepali actors, and a production process that frequently allowed reality to determine what happened next.
Khoriya is screening at Busan International Film Festival

The origins of “Khoriya” go back to 2019, when Singh began making an informal documentary about Nepali migrants working in Indian cities. The subject had personal significance for him: he had grown up around Nepali people, had Nepali classmates, and his brother-in-law is Nepali. Yet he felt this substantial migrant community was rarely discussed within India. When COVID arrived in 2020, the documentary collapsed as Singh lost contact with several of his subjects. The stories, however, remained with him, eventually pushing him toward fiction as another way of exploring the same world.

COVID also entered the film indirectly. The avian-flu outbreak depicted in the story functions partly as a metaphor for the pandemic and for the experience of seeing livelihoods suddenly disappear. Singh points particularly toward Nepali workers occupying some of the least secure positions within poultry businesses, handling animals while facing the greatest physical risks and enjoying little protection. One of his protagonists has actually risen to become a poultry-farm manager, putting a Nepali character unusually in a position of authority, only to watch that status disappear when the outbreak destroys the business.

The constant tension running through “Khoriya” reflects this instability. Singh did not want the characters to appear as people with enough security to stop, evaluate their circumstances and calmly decide what to do next. Their lives simply do not provide that luxury. They are continually moving between jobs, places and problems, reacting to whatever circumstances impose upon them. Handheld camerawork, restless movement and the editing rhythm were all designed around this lack of stability, giving the sense that the characters are heading somewhere without ever knowing exactly where.

The film’s female character is approached very differently. Singh repeatedly films her from behind or avoids presenting her fully because the movie experiences her largely through the young man’s perspective. To him, she is almost a ghost from his past: the person who drew him toward the city but who never completely belongs to him. Singh was also conscious of stereotypes surrounding Nepali women in Delhi, particularly assumptions connecting them with salons, massage parlors and nighttime work. Rather than explaining exactly what she does, he deliberately preserves uncertainty around her life and keeps part of her identity beyond both the protagonist and the audience.

The resulting film is undeniably bleak, although Singh does not consider that a general statement about all Nepali migrants. He knows people who have overcome extremely difficult circumstances and built successful lives through their work. The bleakness instead reflects what he sees in the particular social environment occupied by these characters. As outsiders living within the urban underbelly, they remain especially vulnerable when something goes wrong: they can be blamed first, dismissed first and reminded immediately that they are considered not to belong.

Alcohol consequently appears less as casual recreation than as a way of temporarily escaping a reality over which the characters have little control. Singh clarified that another substance appearing in the story is not a recreational drug but steroids used in an attempt to pass army recruitment requirements. Alcoholism, however, is something he sees as a genuine social problem, particularly among people whose hopes remain alive while their surroundings continually undermine them. For such characters, drinking can become a way of briefly “checking out” from a claustrophobic existence.

One of the film’s most striking sequences, in which the young man’s head is forcibly shaved during army training, comes directly from Singh’s own experience. Coming from an army family and once expected to join the Indian Army himself, he remembers having his long hair shaved before recruitment. He also witnessed hair cutting being used to discipline and humiliate recruits who appeared insufficiently serious. In “Khoriya”, the humiliation acquires another layer because the other recruits laugh specifically when the Nepali character is subjected to it.

Remarkably, the scene itself was largely documentary. Singh filmed at a functioning training center using real army hopefuls and a real coach, without controlling their routine. The production had to arrive during their early-morning training and simply place the actors within the existing environment. Singh told the coach that the protagonist was a new recruit who had not been attending properly and asked what he would normally do. The coach replied that he would shave his head. Singh handed him a clipper and allowed the situation to unfold, even without discussing the decision with the actor beforehand. Afterward, the production took a day off to recalibrate, while the character’s newly shaved appearance ended up changing the rest of the film visually.

Casting presented one of the production’s greatest difficulties. Singh found that established casting networks in Mumbai and Delhi offered very limited access to Nepali and northeastern performers. Four months of street casting followed, particularly in Delhi neighborhoods with significant Nepali populations, but Singh initially encountered understandable suspicion from people who did not know him and had never considered themselves actors. Eventually, he travelled to Sikkim and contacted the National School of Drama’s local repertory. Two performers ultimately resigned from the repertory in order to join the film.

The younger brother was discovered in a considerably less conventional manner. At around 4:30 one morning, Singh was scrolling through Instagram when he encountered an absurd reel that made him laugh. He immediately messaged the young man about meeting for the film, received a response within a minute and quickly became convinced that he had found not simply an actor but the character himself. The performer playing the elder brother brought an even more direct connection to the material, having grown up around a family business involving a momo shop and poultry farm.

That authenticity meant Singh had to surrender some control. Since he was not from the community and did not fully speak the language, he refused to dictate dialogue and linguistic details he could not genuinely understand. Casting director Vinita Chamling Rai and the actors helped shape the language, tone and cultural specificity of individual scenes. A month and a half of workshops allowed them to repeatedly rewrite and perform dialogue until Singh could recognize its emotional rhythm almost musically, even when he could not understand every word literally.

Post-production proved almost as lengthy as the production itself. Because “Khoriya” was shot across separate periods, Singh initially edited the material himself after the first schedule. Following the second shoot, another editor reconstructed and expanded that version over approximately eight months. Selection for an NFDC film lab subsequently brought post-production funding and mentorship from experienced editors, while executive producer Ashim Ahluwalia helped further refine the film’s voice and structure. Altogether, Singh estimates that the editing process lasted roughly a year and a half.

Singh has already begun writing his next project, which moves into very different territory. The film will concern Indian soldiers during World War II, and he is currently taking meetings while preparing to pitch it. He also revealed that he discussed the project with Wim Wenders the previous year, although he is not yet ready to disclose further details.

“Khoriya”, however, remains closely connected to the filmmaker’s original documentary impulse. Its fiction repeatedly opens itself to real locations, real routines and people whose experiences are close to those of the characters. Rather than attempting to speak completely on behalf of a community outside his own, Singh built the production around collaboration, observation and occasionally relinquishing authority. The resulting film reflects characters who rarely control what happens to them, while the filmmaking itself repeatedly allowed an unpredictable reality to enter the frame.
